items.title: Optimizing Muse Spark Open on TPU v7 with SGLang-TorchTPU
items.headline: SGLang-TorchTPU runs all 62 layers of 816B Muse Spark Open as one Pallas megakernel on TPU v7: 1.95 vs 3.78 ms per decode token
items.summary: RadixArk engineers (PyTorch blog, 10 Nov) describe serving Muse Spark Open (816B MoE, ~42B active; 62 MoE layers routing 8 of 256 experts; 46 sliding-window layers over 2,048 tokens plus 16 full-attention layers up to 1M tokens; NVFP4 experts; weightless QK-norm that bounds scores to |43.8|) on one 4-chip Ironwood host with 8-way tensor parallelism. Changes: the whole decoder stack runs as one Pallas program per device, with a ~10-tile dense-weight DMA ring (3.34 TB/s vs 1.13 TB/s for a single stream), expert weights prefetched as soon as routing finishes, two all-gathers per layer folded into the following matmul, the online-softmax running max dropped (safe because QK-norm bounds the scores), split expert loops to cut register spills, an fp8 sequence-on-lane KV layout (256 vs 512 B per token per layer per device), host DRAM as a second KV tier (HiCache) and DFlash2 block speculative decoding verified inside the megakernel.
items.result: Single-request decode 1.95 ms vs 3.78 ms per token for the native path (1.94x), 1.85x at 2 concurrent requests; DFlash2 cuts 3.93 to 1.95 ms; attention microbenchmark 3.9x faster with longer chunks plus no running max; HiCache up to +77% throughput on agent traffic; on a 1M-context agent trace, 433 tok/s per request at 6,101 tok/s per chip up to 25,906 tok/s per chip at 95 tok/s per request. Code at sgl-project/sglang-torchtpu.
items.critique: Vendor-team engineering post, not peer reviewed. The headline speedup is against the team's own native TPU path, not against GPU serving stacks; the TPU-vs-GB200 cost basis is cited but no head-to-head throughput is shown. Gains shrink as concurrency grows. Collective folding, sequence parallelism and dropping the softmax max are not bit-identical and are covered only by unspecified accuracy checks; one figure uses an earlier Muse Spark checkpoint. Posted 10 Nov, slightly outside the 24-hour window, but not covered before.

items.title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
items.headline: Muir (Google) linear attention: 1.8-2.0% lower perplexity than Gated DeltaNet-2 at 166M-1.34B params, same throughput
items.summary: Analyzes gated delta-rule linear attention (Gated DeltaNet-2 has channel-wise decay and separate full-rank erase and write gates) and finds the state is far less sensitive to erasure than to writes, and that slow-decaying state rows grow ~100x larger in norm than fast ones and dominate readout. Muir (1) merges all gates into one low-rank projection with capacity allocated by sensitivity (smaller erase path), spending the saved parameters on a wider FFN; (2) adds a token-dependent matched-filter read gate that reweights state rows; (3) replaces the chunkwise algorithm, which is numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes wide matrix units need, with a stable parallel update (described by the author as a division-free block-Neumann kernel for TPU-style matrix units).
items.result: At 166M-1.34B params: perplexity 1.8-2.0% lower than GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% lower than a Transformer; commonsense accuracy up to +1.9 points; better multi-hop and multi-needle recall at 1.34B; extrapolates from 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift; near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens; throughput matches GDN-2, reaches its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and trains 2.7x faster than the Transformer at 32K.
items.critique: Largest model is 1.34B, so behavior at production scale is untested. Baselines are GDN-2 and a Transformer only; no comparison with Mamba-style SSMs, KDA or hybrid stacks, which is how linear layers are deployed now. Perplexity gains are small (about 2%). No code is linked. The kernel speed claims are TPU-oriented and GPU behavior is not reported. Read from the HF paper page (arXiv was rate-limited); submitted 5 Nov, outside the 24-hour window but not covered before.

items.title: DSpine draft model for Qwen3.8-27B (Tencent)
items.headline: Tencent adds a Qwen3.8-27B DSpine parallel drafter (block 16, 8K sliding window); acceptance 7.83 vs DFlash2 7.55 on Qwen3-8B
items.summary: DSpine is a parallel block drafter for speculative decoding: all positions in a block are drafted in one pass, but at every draft layer each position receives the predicted feature of its predecessor, so the causal chain runs through network depth instead of time. The November README update adds support and draft weights for Qwen3.8-27B (block size 16, 8K sliding window, DSpark-based dynamic verification, ReplaySSM) and Apple Silicon inference via mlx-lm and SGLang-MLX; serving examples use SGLang 0.5.22. Separately, AlphaSignal reports a community GGUF port running the 27B pair at 104.8 tok/s on one RTX 3090 vs 58.2 tok/s with DFlash2 and ~29 tok/s without speculation.
items.result: README (Qwen3-8B target, drafters retrained on Open-PerfectBlend): average acceptance length at T=0 is 7.83 vs DFlash2 7.55, DSpark 7.44, Domino 7.05, DFlash 5.92; at T=1 it is 6.98 vs DSpark 6.65 and DFlash2 6.53. Highest at T=0 on GSM8K (10.55) and MATH-500 (10.30), lowest on MT-Bench (5.63).
items.critique: The README reports acceptance length only, not wall-clock speedup, gives no hardware, and has no EAGLE-3 or MTP baselines; no Qwen3.8-27B numbers are given in the README. The 104.8 tok/s figure comes from secondary coverage of one community member's single-GPU llama.cpp fork test with an undisclosed setup. Exact weight release date is not stated (secondary coverage suggests about 9 Nov); the Hugging Face model card could not be read.

items.title: Training a 1T-Parameter MoE on EU public infrastructure with PyTorch and TorchTitan
items.headline: EUROPA consortium trains a 951.9B-param MoE (32.8B active) on JUPITER GH200s with TorchTitan, 90 to ~1,300 tokens/s per GPU
items.summary: The EUROPA consortium (Domyn, Fraunhofer IAIS/IIS) describes pretraining a 951.9B-total / 32.8B-active MoE (74 layers, hidden 6,144, 384 routed experts top-8, expert hidden 1,792, 256K vocab, 65,536-token sequences) with Muon for ~99.5% of parameters and AdamW for router and embeddings, on the JUPITER supercomputer: 384 GH200s per data-parallel replica (4 replicas, 1,536 GPUs), 384-way FSDP plus 4-way intra-node expert parallelism, no pipeline parallelism. Upstreamed changes include FlexShard for Muon, activation-checkpoint offloading to Grace memory, an unshard_async_op option and a shared RoPE cache.
items.result: Per-GPU throughput rose from 90 to ~1,300 tokens/s. FlexShard for Muon: 441 to 597 tokens/s and optimizer step 41.7 s to 2.2 s; activation offloading: 370 to 508 tokens/s and enabled 64K-token sequences; unshard_async_op: 996 to 1,210 tokens/s with peak reserved memory 88.1 to 74.6 GiB. About 25M tokens per step.
items.critique: Only internal before/after numbers: no MFU, no precision format, no comparison with Megatron or other stacks. Tokens trained, data mix, evaluations, model name and weight release status are not given. Despite the '1T' title the configured model is 951.9B parameters.

items.title: Fast by Default: Compile-Time Heuristics for Helion Kernels
items.headline: Helion now picks kernel configs at compile time with no autotuning: 1.18x handwritten Flash Linear Attention forward on H100
items.summary: Helion, PyTorch's kernel DSL, previously relied on slow autotuning (one paged-attention kernel took 10-25 hours across 72 shapes). New heuristics classify each kernel from its IR (matmul, reduction or pointwise), run a liveness analysis to estimate registers, shared memory and Blackwell tensor memory per CTA, and emit block sizes, num_warps, num_stages, L2 grouping and eviction policies directly; with autotuning on they seed the search with 5-20 configs. Enabled by default for H100 and B200 on the Triton backend; compile cost changes by tens of milliseconds.
items.result: H100, vs handwritten kernels: Flash Linear Attention 1.18x forward / 1.12x with backward (old no-autotune default 0.52x, full autotune 1.26x); vLLM's six CUDA reduction kernels 1.27x (autotune 1.31x, old default 0.58x). Vs torch.compile max-autotune: reductions 1.09x, matmul families 1.88x. Seeding cuts median configs tried to reach within 50% of best from 35.5 to 1.0, but does not improve the final config.
items.critique: Author-run benchmarks on H100 only; constants were tuned on H100/B200 and other backends are untested. Some matmul comparisons are not like-for-like because PyTorch materializes intermediates Helion fuses, and jagged HSTU attention regressed (3.72x to 3.27x). No direct cuBLAS comparison. Heuristics decline kernels with runtime-only extents.

items.title: LowRAM: Low-Rank Keys and Amortised Values for Composable KV Cache Compression at Test-Time
items.headline: LowRAM predicts each head's values from its keys, keeping residuals for worst tokens: 4x value compression, up to 5x decode throughput
items.summary: Observes that within an attention head, values are largely predictable from keys. 'Value cache amortisation' fits a lightweight per-head key-to-value predictor at test time (meta-learned initialization to cut prefill overhead, or fit from scratch for multi-query workloads) and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst. Combined with cross-layer low-rank key compression into an asymmetric pipeline that reconstructs only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, and composable with quantization and eviction.
items.result: 4x near-lossless value compression; close to lossless across three model families; up to 5x higher peak decode throughput at 4x compression; combined with quantization and eviction, 26.9x compression at 94.5% of baseline performance on long contexts.
items.critique: The page does not name the model families, benchmarks or baseline KV methods, so the 'near-lossless' and throughput claims cannot be checked against competitors (e.g. KIVI, xKV) from what was read. Test-time predictor fitting adds prefill cost that is only partly offset by meta-learning; how the 5x throughput was measured (batch, hardware) is unstated. Code is linked (lowram-model/lowram). Published 4 Nov, posted to HF Daily Papers 9 Nov; read from the HF page only.

items.title: SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering
items.headline: SteerDistill: W4A16 LLM agents within one point of BF16 across five agent benchmarks; beats QeRL on tau2-Bench with 67% fewer GPU hours
items.summary: Low-bit agents fail by missing task requirements or environment conditions, which sends them into environment states full-precision runs never reach, so offline distillation data does not cover their failures. SteerDistill is quantization-aware distillation with closed-loop teacher steering: a full-precision teacher guides the quantized student to revise its failed responses and refines the guidance from the student's execution feedback. The student is then trained without guidance to match the steered student's predictions at corrected turns and the teacher's predictions elsewhere.
items.result: Across five agentic benchmarks and three models under W4A16, beats the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67-2.18 points average score and stays within one point of BF16. On tau2-Bench, +1.84 points success rate over QeRL with 67% fewer training GPU hours; successful trajectories are shorter.
items.critique: W4A16 (weight-only 4-bit) is a mild setting where many PTQ methods are already near-lossless, so the margins are small; the abstract does not name the three models or four of the five benchmarks. Requires on-policy environment rollouts with a full-precision teacher, so cost is training-time and environment-dependent. Read from the HF page (arXiv was rate-limited); arXiv date 10 Nov.

items.title: ExecuTorch WebGPU: PyTorch Models on the GPU, in the Browser
items.headline: ExecuTorch gets a WebGPU backend: one .pte runs in browsers and on Metal/Vulkan/D3D12; 4-7x prefill vs its Wasm CPU path
items.summary: A WebGPU backend for ExecuTorch: models exported with torch.export and a WebGPUPartitioner to a .pte file run in WebGPU browsers (Chrome, Safari) via a C++ runtime compiled to WebAssembly, and natively on Metal, Vulkan and D3D12, with WGSL shaders. Demonstrated models include 4-bit Llama 3.2 1B, Qwen2.5-0.5B and Qwen3-0.6B, Gemma 3 1B, SmolVLM, Whisper base and several vision models, plus on-device LoRA/DiReFT fine-tuning.
items.result: Chrome on an Apple M1 Pro, quantized Llama 3.2 1B and Qwen3-0.6B, 128 to 8K context: 4-7x faster prefill and 2-10x faster decode than ExecuTorch's WebAssembly + XNNPACK CPU backend.
items.critique: Only baseline is ExecuTorch's own CPU path, and precision is not matched (fp32 activations on WebGPU vs 8-bit dynamic activations on CPU); no comparison with WebLLM, transformers.js or ONNX Runtime Web. One machine and one browser. The backend is described as early development, with unsupported operators unlisted. Posted 10 Nov.

items.title: Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen
items.headline: Google releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen: $1.50/$7.50 per M tokens, 1M context, 2.5x faster than 3.8 Flash; AA Index 51 vs Argon's 50
items.summary: Google's new fast model, rolling out globally from 12 Nov across the Gemini API/AI Studio, Antigravity, Gemini for business, the Gemini app and Search. Native 1M-token input with up to 1M output tokens, flat pricing across the window, and four thinking levels including a new xhigh tier. Google says it finishes tasks 2.5x faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash at its high default setting and runs 2-2.8x faster with 12-23% fewer tokens in early partner tests.
items.result: Vendor-reported: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index 51 at high (54 at xhigh) vs 50 for Gemini 4 Argon; Terminal-Bench 4.1 57% vs 18.2% for Gemini 3.8 Flash; more than 5x fewer fabricated claims than 3.8 Flash.
items.critique: Closed model with no architecture, parameter or serving details, so nothing to learn about efficiency methods. The speed figures are task-completion times vs Google's own previous model with unstated setup; some comparison baselines (e.g. Orchestrator's 19% faster) are not clearly defined. All benchmarks are self-reported.
